item.title: Matter that learns what matters
item.description: arXiv:2610.34428v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a material learn what deserves its attention? We show that it can in a model optical network, in which action outcomes train a persistent record in each link. The record biases whether a source is consulted and sets how strongly it changes a stored answer, so useful sources gain attention and influence without being identified in advance. The network's experience thus shapes the information available for its future learning. Resonant readouts make this learning fragile: reinforcement can carry a record past resonance, where it persists but its influence weakens. We derive bounds within which relevant signals guide the answer, irrelevant signals are rejected and stored answers remain open to revision. These bounds guide a learning rule that limits reinforcement as records form; in simulations, it acquires useful records and keeps them functional. When relevance changes, an obsolete record can block its own replacement. A local state that strengthens negative writing after unsuccessful actions releases obsolete records and completes the learning sequence more often. How a memory is read should decide how it is written.
item.dc:creator: Natalia G. Berloff

item.title: Waveform proportionality and Taylor's law in networks of Lorenz systems
item.description: arXiv:2505.10159v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Taylor's law (TL), a power-law relationship between the mean and variance of a quantity, has been observed across diverse scientific disciplines. Despite its ubiquity, the underlying mechanisms responsible for TL have not yet been fully elucidated. In particular, the frequent empirical observation of TL with an exponent 2 warrants further investigation. In a previous study, we hypothesized that synchronization contributes to the emergence of TL with an exponent 2. To validate this hypothesis, we employed coupled oscillator models, with each oscillator described by a distinct dynamical system: a food chain model, the R\"ossler system, the Brusselator, and the Lorenz system. Our analytical and numerical results demonstrated that strong coupling leads to a form of synchronization wherein time series become proportional to each other, resulting in TL with an exponent 2. Here, we extend our previous findings for the coupled Lorenz system and provide detailed calculations. We analytically and numerically show that, under strong coupling, waveform proportionality and TL with an exponent 2 emerge for some variables in the globally coupled original, generalized, and hyperchaotic Lorenz systems. Furthermore, we derive a condition under which these properties hold for the original Lorenz system on networks. We then numerically confirm that when heterogeneous oscillators are randomly distributed within the network, waveform proportionality and TL with an exponent 2 emerge across several representative network structures, such as a two-dimensional lattice, random networks, and scale-free networks.
item.dc:creator: Yuzuru Mitsui, Hiroshi Kori

item.title: Recovery Random Walks for Extreme Events on Complex Networks
item.description: arXiv:2609.39377v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Extreme events are widely studied within simple random walk frameworks, where their probability is determined by the network structure and stationary walker distribution. Here, we propose a recovery random walk (RRW) model in which extreme events temporally `freeze' the nodes where they occur for a fixed duration $\Delta$ ($\Delta=0$ recovers the original model), trapping walkers and reducing the effective mobile population, thereby making the model more practical. We derive a first-principles description of this feedback and a delayed differential equation for the frozen-node fraction. This finite freezing produces an initial overshoot, followed by damped oscillatory relaxation to a steady state for the fraction of the frozen nodes. We find that freezing suppresses extreme event probability while preserving its degree dependence dynamics, and suppresses the EE frequency. Further, the analytical prediction for the fraction of the frozen nodes agrees closely with simulations. This model closely reflects real-world scenarios, yielding more practical EE statistics.
item.dc:creator: Karan Singh, Narendran R. V., V. K. Chandrasekar, D. V. Senthilkumar

item.title: The pursuit of happiness
item.description: arXiv:2506.10537v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper studies populations of individuals -- that we call homo-felix -- who maximise an objective function that we call happiness. The happiness of one individual depends on the payoffs that they receive in games they play with their peers as well as on the happiness of the peers they interact with, and on their status. Individuals care more or less about others depending on whether that makes them more or less happy. This paper analyses the ``happiness feedback loops'' that result from these interactions in simple settings. We find that individuals revise their other-regarding attitudes in terms of relative comparisons. In particular, individuals tend to care more about individuals who are happier than them, while spiteful behavior may emerge only under poor socio-economic conditions and is directed towards the worst off individuals. Such general results are illustrated by studying simple 2 x 2 games, where we find that homo-felix can converge to a variety of equilibria which includes but goes beyond Nash equilibria, and in an $n$-persons public good game.
item.dc:creator: Debora Princepe, Onofrio Mazzarisi, Erol Akcay, Simon A. Levin, Matteo Marsili

item.title: Symmetry-breaking in a discrete-choice LQG mean field game
item.description: arXiv:2610.05730v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mean-field games provide a continuum framework for modeling the dynamics of large, interacting populations of non-cooperative agents. This paper studies symmetry-breaking in a finite-horizon, two-choice min-LQG mean-field game in which identical agents with linear stochastic dynamics choose one of two equally desirable terminal destinations, while trading off control effort against social pressure to conform. The model has an odd symmetry between the two destinations and therefore always admits a symmetric, dynamic Nash equilibrium in which the population splits evenly between them, producing a deadlock collective state at final time. Numerical studies have suggested that, as the penalty for social nonconformity increases, this symmetric equilibrium loses stability as a fixed point of an associated scalar, self-consistency map, and asymmetric consensus Nash equilibria emerge, where most agents select the same destination. By analyzing the linearized forward-backward PDE system through the scalar map representation, we provide a proof of this loss of stability of the symmetric equilibrium. Together with the odd symmetry of the map, this implies the existence of symmetry-broken mean-field game equilibria corresponding to consensus on either destination.
item.dc:creator: Ali Akbar Rezaei Lori, Piyush Grover

item.title: A learner-free swarm reaches the explore-exploit equilibrium: A self-organized attractor approximating the reinforcement-learning solution
item.description: arXiv:2610.25113v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The explore-exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). In its multi-agent, resource-sharing form the optimum is not a scalar-return maximum but an equilibrium allocation -- the ideal-free distribution (IFD), the Nash equilibrium of a congestion game. We show that a minimal foraging swarm reaches the shape of this equilibrium as a self-organized attractor -- foragers in proportion to resource richness (matching slope 0.94) -- with no learner, no trained parameters, and no payoff or reward read anywhere in its dynamics. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; removing the coupling of recruitment to movement collapses the matching (slope 0.08). The reinforcement learning is at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule. The swarm reaches this equilibrium rather than learning it, attaining its shape but not the exact equilibrium: it stays measurably exploitable (Nash-gap 0.58 versus ~0.01 for a converged learner). Against PPO learners (feedforward, centralized-critic, and graph message-passing) trained in the same sensing-limited environment, the reward-free swarm at zero training matches the IFD gradient more faithfully than any learner (slope ~1 vs 0.69-0.91) and ties the best learner's harvest where clustered (both plateau at ~0.80 of an oracle ceiling), while the learner collects more where resource is scarce (0.33 vs 0.22) and holds tighter per-capita intake. Learning thus buys precision and transfer, not a better allocation; neither message passing nor a centralized critic exceeds it at this budget. We read this not as beating RL, but as evidence that a minimal swarm's physics reaches the equilibrium RL seeks without a learner, a reward, or a trained parameter. A companion paper develops the mechanism.
item.dc:creator: Galen J. Wilkerson

item.title: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle
item.description: arXiv:2610.27235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket (a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior) can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, reproduce, and die. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well. A flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior. Flux removes only part of the linear dependence, and a nonlinear test shows that conditioning on flux increases the dependence. We argue that this is because flux is a statistical collider. Conditioning on the boundary's own concentration state screens about a fifth of the nonlinear dependence. The dependence is concentrated within about one organism radius of the boundary. A band of the surrounding field of that thickness does screen the interior from the exterior beyond it, as any short-range field would; this is not evidence of inference.
item.dc:creator: John E Pearson
